description: Incentives, cloud cost and FinOps, business-case finance, macro cycles and game theory for architects who must justify, fund and negotiate platform decisions.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::01 Incentives & Microeconomics
notes.front: Why should platform decisions use marginal cost rather than average cost?
notes.back: Marginal cost is the cost of one more unit. Averages spread fixed costs and hide the step changes, and decisions are made at the margin (one more tenant, one more region).
notes.extra: Example: One more namespace on a running cluster costs almost nothing; the first cluster in a new region costs a control plane, networking and on-call. Average-cost pricing overcharges small teams.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::01 Incentives & Microeconomics
notes.front: What is opportunity cost?
notes.back: The value of the best alternative you gave up. The real cost of a choice is what you could otherwise have done with the same resources.
notes.extra: Example: Three engineers building an in-house CI for six months: the cost isn't their salaries (paid either way) but the migrations and reliability work that didn't happen.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::01 Incentives & Microeconomics
notes.front: A team spends three engineer-months building an in-house tool that a $20k/year product would replace. What is the opportunity cost?
notes.back: The best alternative use of those three engineer-months (e.g. features not shipped), not just their salary. Compare that against the product's price.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::01 Incentives & Microeconomics
notes.front: What is the principal-agent problem?
notes.back: A principal delegates to an agent whose incentives and information differ. Where interests diverge the agent acts for themselves, and the principal can't fully observe it.
notes.extra: Example: A vendor's solutions architect is an agent for the vendor, not for you. Read every recommendation asking 'who pays this person, and for what?'

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::01 Incentives & Microeconomics
notes.front: What is moral hazard?
notes.back: Taking more risk, or consuming more, because someone else bears the cost of the outcome.
notes.extra: Example: Teams over-provision because the central IT budget pays. Chargeback and showback exist mainly to remove this hazard.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::01 Incentives & Microeconomics
notes.front: Why does a team with an unlimited shared cloud budget over-provision, and which concept is this? How would you fix it?
notes.back: Moral hazard: the team gets the benefit while the central budget bears the cost. Fix by making cost visible or chargeable (showback, chargeback) or by setting quotas.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::01 Incentives & Microeconomics
notes.front: Why do teams 'irrationally' refuse a platform that would save the company money?
notes.back: They're usually responding rationally to incentives: migration cost and risk land on the product team, savings land on a central budget nobody on the team is measured on.
notes.extra: Example: Fix the incentive (centrally funded migration, chargeback, adoption in team goals) before blaming the culture.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::01 Incentives & Microeconomics
notes.front: What is incentive-caused bias?
notes.back: People sincerely come to believe what it is in their interest to believe. It isn't conscious dishonesty; it works below awareness.
notes.extra: Example: A consultancy that resells one cloud will, in good faith, find that cloud the best fit. Discount advice in proportion to the advisor's stake.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::01 Incentives & Microeconomics
notes.front: What are diminishing marginal returns?
notes.back: Each extra unit of input adds less output than the previous one, other inputs held fixed.
notes.extra: Example: 99% → 99.9% availability is cheap; 99.99% → 99.999% can cost more than everything before it. Ask where on the curve you are.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::01 Incentives & Microeconomics
notes.front: Why does making an internal service free make demand explode?
notes.back: At a price of zero, demand is limited only by effort, not value. Any positive price, even small, forces a value-vs-cost comparison and changes behaviour sharply.
notes.analogy: An all-you-can-eat buffet: plates come back half full.
notes.extra: Example: Free storage grows without bound: nobody deletes old snapshots. A modest internal price per GB-month makes cleanup someone's rational choice.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::01 Incentives & Microeconomics
notes.front: What is the market for lemons (information asymmetry)?
notes.back: When buyers can't tell good from bad, they pay an average price; sellers of good products leave and quality collapses. Signals and guarantees exist to fix this.
notes.analogy: Used-car buyers who can't spot lemons offer an average price, so owners of good cars stop selling.
notes.extra: Example: Reference calls, PoCs and exit clauses are how you buy information from a vendor. A vendor that refuses a PoC is signalling.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::01 Incentives & Microeconomics
notes.front: Why do vendor guarantees (service-level agreements, free trials, open-source code) help sell a product when buyers fear a market for lemons?
notes.back: They are costly signals a poor-quality seller could not afford to offer, so they let buyers tell good from bad and keep good sellers in the market.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::01 Incentives & Microeconomics
notes.front: Coase: why do firms exist, and how does that frame build-vs-buy?
notes.back: Using the market has transaction costs (search, contracting, monitoring, enforcement). A firm does internally what's cheaper to coordinate internally. Build-vs-buy compares the two coordination costs.
notes.extra: Example: A managed database removes internal ops coordination but adds contract, integration and vendor-management cost.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::01 Incentives & Microeconomics
notes.front: What are switching costs, and why do they matter in both directions for a platform architect?
notes.back: The cost a customer bears to change supplier (migration, retraining, risk); high switching costs give the supplier pricing power. You want them low for teams adopting your platform and must watch them high with your vendors.
notes.extra: Example: Estimate the exit cost before signing and keep it visible in the architecture.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::01 Incentives & Microeconomics
notes.front: What is mechanism design, and why is it the real job of a platform team?
notes.back: Designing the rules of the game so participants pursuing their own interests produce the outcome you want: make good behaviour the dominant strategy instead of asking for it.
notes.extra: Example: Golden paths that are easier than the alternative, chargeback that makes rightsizing rational, quotas that make fairness automatic. Constant persuasion means the mechanism is wrong.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::02 Cloud Cost & FinOps
notes.front: What are unit economics, and why do they beat totals?
notes.back: Cost and revenue per fundamental unit (customer, request, GB stored). Totals hide whether growth is profitable; unit figures reveal it.
notes.extra: Example: A cloud bill up 40% is fine if requests rose 80%; a flat bill with falling traffic is a problem.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::02 Cloud Cost & FinOps
notes.front: What makes an architect's cost argument fundable?
notes.back: A defensible number: 'about X/month at current load, Y per extra 10k users; the alternative costs Z', honest about its assumptions. Approximately right beats precisely wrong.
notes.extra: Example: 'Event-driven adds €4k/month in queues but removes a €9k/month replica' gets funded; 'event-driven is more scalable' doesn't.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::02 Cloud Cost & FinOps
notes.front: Fixed vs variable cost in cloud: what's the difference?
notes.back: Fixed costs don't change with volume (commitments, platform salaries). Variable costs scale with use (on-demand compute, per-request pricing, egress).
notes.extra: Example: A three-year commitment turns variable cost into fixed: cheaper at steady load, expensive if traffic halves.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::02 Cloud Cost & FinOps
notes.front: What is operating leverage, and when should a workload avoid it?
notes.back: The share of fixed in total cost. High operating leverage means results swing strongly with volume, up and down. Avoid it when demand is uncertain; stay variable.
notes.extra: Example: Startups with unproven demand should stay on-demand; a stable enterprise workload should commit.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::02 Cloud Cost & FinOps
notes.front: Demand falls 40% after you signed a large three-year reserved block. What happens to your unit economics, and which concept explains it?
notes.back: Cost is mostly fixed, so cost per unit of work rises and margins fall sharply. This is high operating leverage working in reverse.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::02 Cloud Cost & FinOps
notes.front: How do you calculate the break-even utilisation of a reserved or committed-use discount?
notes.back: Break-even = reserved price / on-demand price. Commit only if expected utilisation over the term is clearly above it.
notes.extra: Example: 35% discount → break-even 65% of hours. Base it on the last three months of actual usage, and don't commit at 66% expected: leave a margin of safety.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::02 Cloud Cost & FinOps
notes.front: A one-year commitment costs 60% of the on-demand price, but the workload runs only 50% of the time. Should you commit? Why?
notes.back: No. Break-even utilisation is 60%. Committing costs 60 per unit of time for all hours; on-demand costs 100 for half the hours, which is 50 overall.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::02 Cloud Cost & FinOps
notes.text: The FinOps lifecycle: Inform ({{c1::visibility, allocation, tagging}}) → Optimise ({{c2::rightsizing, commitments, architecture}}) → Operate ({{c3::governance, budgets, continuous improvement}}). It is a cycle, not a project.
notes.extra: Common mistake: optimising before Inform is done, e.g. buying reservations before knowing which team owns the workload.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::02 Cloud Cost & FinOps
notes.front: List every phase of the FinOps (Financial Operations) lifecycle and what each one does.
notes.back:
Inform: visibility, allocation, tagging.
Optimise: rightsizing, commitments, architecture.
Operate: governance, budgets, continuous improvement. Then repeat.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::02 Cloud Cost & FinOps
notes.front: Showback vs chargeback: what's the difference in effect?
notes.back: Showback: teams see their cost, no money moves; it informs. Chargeback: cost is transferred to the team's budget; it changes incentives.
notes.extra: Example: Start with showback to get allocation right, then move to chargeback.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::02 Cloud Cost & FinOps
notes.front: Why can showback alone fail to cut cloud waste?
notes.back: No money moves, so teams aren't measured on the cost and have little incentive to act on it. Chargeback changes incentives; showback only informs.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::02 Cloud Cost & FinOps
notes.front: Why is cloud egress priced high and ingress free?
notes.back: It's a switching-cost mechanism: ingress increases lock-in, egress reduces it. Egress is priced far above its cost.
notes.extra: Example: Moving 500 TB out can cost tens of thousands of euro, quietly raising the exit cost of every design that stores data there. Model exit cost in design reviews.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::02 Cloud Cost & FinOps
notes.front: How does utilisation change the effective price of a resource?
notes.back: Effective cost per unit of useful work = list price / utilisation. At 20% utilisation you pay five times list price per unit of work.
notes.extra: Example: A €100/month VM at 15% CPU is ~€667/month of useful compute. Low on-prem utilisation (10–20%) is why cloud economics worked at all.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::02 Cloud Cost & FinOps
notes.front: What is the most common FinOps trap involving engineering time?
notes.back: Spending expensive engineering time to save cheap infrastructure. Prioritise by (monthly saving × lifetime) / engineering cost.
notes.extra: Example: A day of work that removes €2,000/month idle capacity pays back in days; a month shaving 5% off a €3,000 bill never pays back.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::02 Cloud Cost & FinOps
notes.front: What is owner earnings, and what is the platform analogue?
notes.back: Buffett's measure: earnings plus non-cash charges, minus the capital spending needed just to maintain competitive position. Platform analogue: value delivered minus the maintenance needed to stand still (upgrades, patching, cert rotation).
notes.extra: A platform whose maintenance cost equals its delivered value has zero owner earnings.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::02 Cloud Cost & FinOps
notes.front: Why does the marginal cost of an additional tenant decide whether a platform has software or services economics?
notes.back: Near-zero marginal cost: cost stays flat while value scales (software). Roughly proportional infrastructure and human effort per tenant: cost scales with value (services, lower margins).
notes.extra: Example: Shared multi-tenant clusters vs cluster-per-tenant. The second can be right for isolation, but it caps the value the platform team can create.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::02 Cloud Cost & FinOps
notes.front: Why must you know a managed service's billing dimension before designing with it?
notes.back: The dimension (per request, GB-month, vCPU-hour, provisioned unit, egress GB) decides which architectures are cheap; the same workload can differ by an order of magnitude.
notes.extra: Example: Functions billed per invocation and millisecond are cheap for bursty work, expensive for a steady 24/7 loop. Match workload shape to pricing shape.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::03 Business Cases & Corporate Finance
notes.front: What is Net Present Value (NPV), and how is it calculated?
notes.back: The sum of future cash flows discounted to today, minus the initial investment: \( \text{NPV} = \sum_t \frac{CF_t}{(1+r)^t} - C_0 \). Positive creates value; negative destroys it.
notes.extra: Example: €600k migration saving €200k/yr for 5 years: NPV ≈ +€158k at 10%, ≈ −€2k at 20%. The discount rate decides the outcome.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::03 Business Cases & Corporate Finance
notes.front: What does the discount rate represent, and how do you pick one for an internal business case?
notes.back: How much less future money is worth than money now: the cost of capital plus a risk premium. Internally, finance sets it as a hurdle rate (often 8–15%); ask, don't invent.
notes.extra: Example: Present the case at finance's rate and show what happens at a higher one.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::03 Business Cases & Corporate Finance
notes.front: What happens to the NPV of a platform investment whose savings arrive mostly in years 5 to 8 if the hurdle rate rises from 8% to 15%? Why?
notes.back: NPV falls, possibly below zero. Higher discount rates shrink distant cash flows most, so back-loaded projects are the first to fail.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::03 Business Cases & Corporate Finance
notes.front: What is the Internal Rate of Return (IRR), and what is its main pitfall?
notes.back: The discount rate at which NPV = 0; if it beats the hurdle rate, the project creates value. It misleads with irregular cash flows or very different project sizes, so pair it with NPV.
notes.extra: Example: The €600k / €200k-per-year migration has an IRR of ~20%: attractive at a 12% hurdle, not at 25%.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::03 Business Cases & Corporate Finance
notes.front: What is payback period, and why is it often the most persuasive number?
notes.back: Time until cumulative savings equal the investment. Crude (ignores time value and everything after payback) but intuitive and hard to argue with.
notes.extra: Example: €600k saving €200k/yr: three years. Executives often have an implicit maximum of 18–36 months.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::03 Business Cases & Corporate Finance
notes.front: How can a project with a short payback period still have a negative NPV?
notes.back: Payback ignores everything after the break-even point. If savings stop soon afterwards, or exit and refresh costs come later, total discounted value can be negative.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::03 Business Cases & Corporate Finance
notes.front: What is Total Cost of Ownership (TCO), and what is most often left out?
notes.back: All costs over the life: acquisition, licences, infrastructure, operations, training, integration, upgrades, compliance, exit. Most often omitted: people's time and migration out.
notes.extra: Example: 'Free' self-hosted open source needing 0.3 of an engineer for upgrades and on-call costs ~€30k/year before hardware.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::03 Business Cases & Corporate Finance
notes.front: CapEx vs OpEx: what's the difference, and why does the CFO care?
notes.back: CapEx buys an asset that's depreciated over years, so only the depreciation hits annual profit. OpEx is expensed immediately in full. Cloud converts CapEx into OpEx.
notes.extra: Example: €1.2M hardware over four years shows €300k/yr expense; €350k/yr cloud spend reduces reported profit in full every year.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::03 Business Cases & Corporate Finance
notes.front: Why does cloud spending hurt EBITDA, and why does that matter politically?
notes.back: EBITDA excludes depreciation, so owned hardware barely touches it while cloud OpEx reduces it fully. Firms valued or bonused on EBITDA are biased toward owning hardware even when cloud wins on NPV.
notes.extra: This is the principal-agent problem in accounting form: know which metric your CFO is measured on.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::03 Business Cases & Corporate Finance
notes.front: What is a margin of safety in a business case?
notes.back: Building the case on conservative assumptions, so the decision stays right even if estimates are significantly wrong.
notes.extra: Example: If it only works at €200k/yr savings and you estimate €210k, don't propose it. If it still clears the hurdle at €140k, propose it and say so.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::03 Business Cases & Corporate Finance
notes.front: Why does every business case need a cost-of-doing-nothing baseline?
notes.back: The status quo is not free: ageing hardware, renewals, growing ops load, security exposure. Without pricing it, your proposal is compared against an imaginary zero-cost option.
notes.extra: Example: 'Do nothing' on an end-of-life platform means an emergency migration in two years, rising support prices and incident cost.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::03 Business Cases & Corporate Finance
notes.front: Why does fully depreciated on-prem hardware look free, and why is that misleading?
notes.back: Its book value is zero, so it shows no depreciation charge. It still costs power, space, support and staff time, and carries rising failure risk.
notes.extra: Example: A five-year-old storage array: add extended support, power, the two engineers who can run it, and no spare parts. Not free.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::03 Business Cases & Corporate Finance
notes.front: What is Return on Invested Capital (ROIC), and what is the platform version?
notes.back: Operating profit after tax / capital invested: value generated per unit of capital, regardless of size. Platform version: quantified value delivered / (team cost + infrastructure).
notes.extra: Example: Avoiding €400k/year of cost on a €1.5M budget is a poor return; the same result from a team a third the size is excellent.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::03 Business Cases & Corporate Finance
notes.front: What is sensitivity analysis, and how much does a business case need?
notes.back: Varying key assumptions one at a time (±20–30%) to see which ones change the decision. Usually only one or two matter; those are the ones to defend.
notes.extra: Example: If only the effort estimate can flip the result, propose a phased approach that reduces that uncertainty first.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::03 Business Cases & Corporate Finance
notes.front: Why are long-horizon savings in a DCF untrustworthy?
notes.back: Discounting shrinks distant cash flows, but not enough to offset how little you know about them. Year-eight savings are guesses dressed as numbers.
notes.extra: Example: Present three to five years, state that the rest is unknowable, and prefer options that keep future choices open.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::03 Business Cases & Corporate Finance
notes.front: Profit vs cash: where does the difference bite in cloud contracts?
notes.back: Profit is an accounting result over a period; cash is what's in the bank. A cheaper-overall option can still be a cash problem.
notes.extra: Example: A three-year all-upfront reservation minimises total cost but consumes cash now. Ask finance which constraint binds: cost or cash.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::03 Business Cases & Corporate Finance
notes.front: How do budgets actually get approved in a large organisation?
notes.back: Annual cycle: requests go in months before the fiscal year, finance consolidates, leadership trades off, the result is locked. A proposal needs a sponsor with budget authority, finance's format, and timing before the window closes.
notes.extra: Example: With a January fiscal year, planning often closes in September–October; a November proposal waits a year or displaces something approved.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::04 Macro, Cycles & Bubbles
notes.front: Trace the chain by which rising interest rates change your employer's spending on engineering. Which businesses are hit hardest, and why?
notes.back: Higher rates raise the discount rate, so businesses whose value lies far in the future (growth tech) lose most. Valuation changes reach hiring, budgets and risk appetite within months.
notes.extra: Example: 2022 rate rises: valuations fell, layoffs followed, and FinOps became a board topic.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::04 Macro, Cycles & Bubbles
notes.front: Why did the zero-interest-rate decade shape engineering culture?
notes.back: Near-free capital meant a near-zero hurdle rate: growth at almost any cost, efficiency a low priority. When rates rose, the same behaviour became unaffordable.
notes.extra: Example: Over-provisioning, redundant tools and no cost allocation are ZIRP-era decisions that much FinOps work now unwinds.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::04 Macro, Cycles & Bubbles
notes.front: What are the business cycle phases, and what does each mean for infrastructure proposals?
notes.back: Expansion (easy budgets) → peak (over-hiring, over-building) → contraction (freezes, cost focus) → trough (consolidation). In contraction, cost-saving migrations get approved fast and vendors are flexible.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::04 Macro, Cycles & Bubbles
notes.front: Nominal vs real: why does it matter for vendor contracts?
notes.back: Nominal is the currency number; real is adjusted for inflation. An annual escalator of 5–8% is a real-terms price rise when inflation is 2%.
notes.extra: Example: Negotiate the escalator, not just the base price. A 3% raise in 6% inflation is a real pay cut.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::04 Macro, Cycles & Bubbles
notes.front: Monetary vs fiscal policy: which drives which IT budgets?
notes.back: Monetary: central-bank interest rates and money supply; acts fast on asset prices and private-sector spend. Fiscal: government taxes and spending; drives public-sector budgets and political cycles.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::04 Macro, Cycles & Bubbles
notes.text: Kindleberger–Minsky bubble stages: displacement ({{c1::a genuine new opportunity}}) → boom → euphoria ({{c2::'this time is different'}}) → profit-taking → panic ({{c3::prices collapse as everyone sells at once}}).
notes.extra: Watch data-centre and accelerator capex for the same pattern.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::04 Macro, Cycles & Bubbles
notes.front: Without looking at the stages above, name every stage of a Kindleberger–Minsky bubble in order.
notes.back: Displacement (a real new opportunity), boom, euphoria ('this time is different'), profit-taking, panic.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::04 Macro, Cycles & Bubbles
notes.front: What is reflexivity, and how does it explain bubble overshoot?
notes.back: Prices don't just reflect fundamentals, they change them: rising prices ease credit, which funds growth, which justifies the prices, until the loop reverses.
notes.extra: Example: A hot tool gets funding → marketing and hiring → adoption → more funding. Judge a tool by what it does when the funding stops.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::04 Macro, Cycles & Bubbles
notes.front: What do bubbles leave behind, and what is the lesson for today's infrastructure build-out?
notes.back: Speculative over-building ruins investors but leaves infrastructure that later becomes cheap: railway mania, 1990s dark fibre carrying the 2000s web.
notes.extra: Example: Some AI data-centre builders won't earn a return, but the capacity will exist. Design for portability to benefit when compute prices fall.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::04 Macro, Cycles & Bubbles
notes.front: What is creative destruction, and what does it imply for architecture bets?
notes.back: Innovation destroys existing businesses while creating new ones, so moats in fast-moving industries are unstable. The layers that lasted (TCP/IP, SQL, POSIX, HTTP) were standards, not products.
notes.extra: Bet on stable layers; keep products swappable.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::04 Macro, Cycles & Bubbles
notes.front: What is compounding, and why does time matter more than rate?
notes.back: Returns are reinvested and earn returns themselves, so growth is exponential. 7% for 40 years multiplies capital ~15×.
notes.extra: Example: Skills and reputation compound: a year learning finance early in an architecture career pays out on every business case after.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::04 Macro, Cycles & Bubbles
notes.front: Why is a 2% yearly drag (fees, or tech debt that grows each year) serious over 30 years?
notes.back: Losses compound too: 0.98 to the power 30 is about 0.55, so roughly 45% of the value is gone. Small persistent rates matter over long horizons.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::05 Game Theory & Vendor Strategy
notes.front: What is the prisoner's dilemma, and where does it appear between teams?
notes.back: Both parties would gain by cooperating, but each does better by defecting whatever the other does, so both defect and both lose. The structure produces the outcome.
notes.extra: Example: Two teams would gain from a shared platform but the first mover bears the cost, so both wait. Change the payoffs: fund the first mover.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::05 Game Theory & Vendor Strategy
notes.front: Two teams each hoard shared cluster capacity, which leaves both worse off (a prisoner's dilemma). Name three ways to move them to cooperation.
notes.back: Change the payoffs (quotas, chargeback), make the interaction repeated so reputation matters, or add enforcement or transparency so defection is visible.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::05 Game Theory & Vendor Strategy
notes.front: What is a Nash equilibrium?
notes.back: A set of strategies where no player gains by changing only their own strategy. Stable, but not necessarily good for anyone.
notes.extra: Example: Every team running its own CI and monitoring is often a Nash equilibrium. Escaping needs a coordinated move or an outside actor changing payoffs: the platform team's job.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::05 Game Theory & Vendor Strategy
notes.front: What did Axelrod's tournaments show about repeated games, and what does it mean for vendors?
notes.back: Tit-for-tat won: cooperate first, retaliate once when defected on, forgive, be transparent. When the game continues, reputation makes cooperation rational.
notes.extra: Example: Squeezing a vendor to a loss-making price gets you a weaker account team and no favours in the next incident. Be firm, proportionate and forgiving.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::05 Game Theory & Vendor Strategy
notes.front: How should an architect think about vendor lock-in?
notes.back: Lock-in is a switching cost, which is a price, not a sin. The mistake is accepting it unknowingly: estimate the exit cost, judge it against the benefit, and keep the estimate current.
notes.extra: Example: At renewal the vendor prices up to your migration cost, because they can estimate it too. Deliberate lock-in with a known price is a valid decision.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::05 Game Theory & Vendor Strategy
notes.front: In game-theory terms, why do standards win or lose?
notes.back: Adoption is a coordination game: everyone cares more about being on the same standard than about which one. Early expectations become self-fulfilling, then network effects lock in the winner.
notes.extra: Example: Kubernetes won partly because early backing made everyone expect it to win. Betting on the standard with momentum is usually right.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::05 Game Theory & Vendor Strategy
notes.front: What is a Schelling point (focal point)?
notes.back: An option people converge on without communicating because it is obvious or salient. Without a coordinator, the focal point wins.
notes.extra: Example: Neutral open standards (OCI images, OpenTelemetry) win when vendors must agree without one of them winning. Internally, the most visible team's tool becomes focal.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::05 Game Theory & Vendor Strategy
notes.front: What is a credible commitment, and how do you use one in negotiation?
notes.back: A commitment that visibly removes your ability to back down, making threats or promises believable.
notes.analogy: Burning your boats on the beach.
notes.extra: Example: 'We'll migrate if the price isn't cut' is cheap talk. A signed pilot with a competitor or a board-approved migration budget is a commitment.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::05 Game Theory & Vendor Strategy
notes.front: Zero-sum vs positive-sum: which is a multi-year vendor deal, and why does it matter?
notes.back: Usually positive-sum: parties can enlarge the pie by trading things they value differently. Treating it as zero-sum leaves value on the table.
notes.extra: Example: Trade a longer commitment (vendor values) for a lower rate plus named support engineers (you value).

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::05 Game Theory & Vendor Strategy
notes.front: What is a chicken game, and how does it explain standards wars?
notes.back: Each side wants the other to give way; if neither does, both lose badly. The winner is whoever credibly appears unable to swerve.
notes.extra: Example: Sony built Blu-ray into every PlayStation 3, an installed base it couldn't abandon. Two competing internal platforms are a chicken game leadership must end.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::05 Game Theory & Vendor Strategy
notes.front: What is the winner's curse?
notes.back: When the item's value is uncertain, the winning bidder is the one who most overestimated it, so winning suggests you overpaid.
notes.extra: Example: The RFP winner on price usually underestimated the work: expect change orders and a weak team. A suspiciously low bid should lower your confidence.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::05 Game Theory & Vendor Strategy
notes.front: Why is the vendor with the lowest bid in a competitive tender a risk, and which concept explains it?
notes.back: Winner's curse: the winner is often the bidder who most underestimated the cost, and may recoup it later through change requests or cutting corners.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::05 Game Theory & Vendor Strategy
notes.front: What is signalling, and where does it appear in architecture work?
notes.back: Conveying private information through costly actions that wouldn't pay if the information were false. Cheap signals are ignored; costly ones are believed.
notes.extra: Example: A costed business case is credible because it is expensive to write; a one-line budget request is cheap talk.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::05 Game Theory & Vendor Strategy
notes.front: How does backward induction apply to contract renewals?
notes.back: Reason from the final move backward. At renewal the vendor prices just below your migration cost, so a good year-3 renewal needs a real alternative by year 2 and portability decisions in year 1.
notes.extra: The renewal is decided at signing.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::05 Game Theory & Vendor Strategy
notes.front: What is Munger's inversion principle, applied to negotiations and designs?
notes.back: Instead of asking how to succeed, ask what would guarantee failure, and avoid that.
notes.extra: Example: Before a vendor negotiation, list what would make it a bad deal (no exit clause, uncapped escalators, unclear data ownership) and negotiate those out first.

notes.deck: Economics for Architects::05 Game Theory & Vendor Strategy
notes.front: How should you value a concession a vendor offers?
notes.back: By its cost to them and its value to you, not by how it's presented. Concessions that cost them nothing (unused licences, 'free' training) are anchoring devices.
notes.extra: Example: '20% extra storage free' vs 'annual escalator capped at 3%': take the second; don't let the first move the price.
